text: On to section four and principle four: the same pair on a menu and a tick box. As always, small first. A fruit menu and an agree box. A drop-down menu is a select tag, and a tick box is an input tag with type equals checkbox. Both can be controlled with the same idea. When the page opens, the menu shows orange and the box is not ticked. Figure 19 puts it on screen. A browser window at localhost:5173 with a menu labeled fruit that reads orange. Below it sits a small empty square with the words I agree next to it. And now the code behind it. The menu uses value like a text box. The tick box uses checked instead. In App.jsx, line one imports useState from React. Line four makes fruit with its setter setFruit, and it starts as orange. Line five makes agree with setAgree, and that one starts as false. Then on line 11, the select tag gets value equals fruit in curly braces, and its onChange takes e arrow setFruit with e.target.value, so the chosen option comes from state. Lines 12 to 14 are the three option tags: apple, banana, and orange, each with its own value. And on line 18, the input with type equals checkbox gets checked equals agree in curly braces. Its onChange calls setAgree with e.target.checked, so the tick comes from state, too. Line 19 is just the words I agree. The user picks banana and ticks the box. In figure 20, it's the same page, but the menu now reads banana and the little square next to I agree has a tick in it. It is the same whiteboard as before. Now the board holds a chosen word and a ticked square, and only state writes them. So what does value mean on a menu? On a select tag, value says which option is chosen. It must match the value of one of the options inside. And each option tag has two texts. The text between its tags, such as banana, is what the user reads. Its value, such as banana with a small B, is the string the menu reports to our code. So the user reads Banana with a capital B, but our code receives banana with a small B. Where did that string come from? The browser supplies it. It goes like this. The user picks banana. The menu's value becomes the value of that option, which is banana. React calls onChange, and e.target.value is banana. setFruit saves banana, and React writes it back into the menu, so banana stays chosen. Next, a rule worth remembering: Never mark an option as selected. In plain HTML, you choose the starting option by writing selected on that option. A developer who knows HTML might write something like this, a select tag with two option tags inside. The first is delivery. The second is payment, and that one carries the word selected. That's the plain HTML habit, and it's marked wrong because React does not support it. React does not support selected on an option. The menu still opens on payment, but React prints a red error in the console. The error tells you to use value or default value on the select instead. The React way puts the choice on the select itself. So the select tag gets value equals payment in quotes and an onChange that calls setTopic with e.target.value. The two option tags, delivery and payment, stay plain with no selected anywhere. React chooses the option whose value matches. React reads value on the select and chooses the option whose value matches. When the menu only needs a starting choice and no state, use default value on the select instead. It works the same way as default value on a text box. And what does checked mean on a tick box? A tick box has no text to show. It is either ticked or not. So it does not use value. It uses checked, a React prop that holds true or false. After every render, React makes the box ticked or unticked to match. In lesson 18, a tick box without checked kept its own tick inside the browser. That box was uncontrolled. With checked from state, React decides the tick, and the box becomes controlled. The handler reads e.target.checked, which the browser supplies. It is the tick right after the click. True if the box is now ticked and false if not. For a tick box that only needs a starting tick, React has defaultChecked, which works like default value. And a tick box with checked but no onChange freezes, too, just like the frozen text box of principle three. React prints the same read-only error, but this time it names checked and defaultChecked.
